title: Normocytic and macrocytic anemias
covers: The reticulocyte-and-MCV approach to anemia, then the normocytic causes (chronic disease, kidney disease, pure red cell aplasia) and the macrocytic causes (B12 and folate deficiency, myelodysplasia, alcohol and liver disease, hypothyroidism).

items.p: Anemia is a low red cell mass or hemoglobin: more than 2 SD below the mean for age and sex. Age, sex, Tanner stage, altitude and heredity shift the normal value.
The number is judged against need. A hemoglobin of 7.5 g/dL is normal in a 2-month-old premature infant; 14 g/dL is anemic in a 2-year-old with cyanotic heart disease.
WHO 2024 cutoff for men: hemoglobin under 13 g/dL or hematocrit under 39%.

items.note: The slide gives the WHO cutoff for women as under 11.9 g/dL (hematocrit under 36%). WHO states 12.0 g/dL for non-pregnant women; worth checking with the lecturer.

items.p: Think of mechanism (production, loss, breakdown) and cell size together. Three things matter most: the history, the CBC with reticulocytes, and the smear.

ul: Reticulocytes raised: hemolysis or blood loss
Reticulocytes normal or low: sort by MCV

table: Reticulocytes (absolute count over 100,000 = bleeding or hemolysis)

items.p: A high RDW makes iron deficiency likely.
Red cells mature in the marrow for about 3 weeks and live 120 days. As anemia deepens, reticulocytes leave the marrow earlier and circulate longer (1 day at a hematocrit of 45%, 2.5 days at 15%).
Also called anemia of inflammation. Seen with infection, inflammation and cancer, and also obesity, diabetes, heart failure, critical illness and severe trauma.
IL-6 makes the liver release hepcidin. Hepcidin blocks ferroportin in the duodenum and in macrophages, so plasma iron falls within hours.
Hemoglobin 7–11 g/dL, normal MCV (microcytic when long-standing), low reticulocytes.
MCV, serum iron and transferrin saturation can be low in both.

ul: Treat the underlying disease. The aim is fewer symptoms, not a normal hemoglobin.
No iron unless the patient is truly iron deficient
Transfuse for hemoglobin under 7 g/dL, or for symptoms at any level

items.p: Normochromic, normocytic, low reticulocytes. The smear is usually normal; echinocytes appear only in rare severe cases.

ul: Less erythropoietin
Hepcidin not cleared by the kidney
Uremic inhibitors of the marrow, and shorter red cell survival
Marrow fibrosis in some, from secondary hyperparathyroidism

items.p: On dialysis, correct iron deficiency first; then an ESA is first line. Target hemoglobin 10–11.5 g/dL.
Only the red cell line fails: severe anemia, reticulocytes often under 10,000/µL, and almost no erythroid precursors in the marrow.

ul: Congenital: Diamond–Blackfan anemia (usually a high MCV)
Acquired: thymoma, CLL and other blood cancers, solid tumors, HIV, EBV, hepatitis, autoimmune disease, antibodies to EPO after ESA treatment, myelodysplasia
Parvovirus B19 kills red cell precursors directly. Giant proerythroblasts in the marrow suggest it but do not prove it: confirm by PCR.

items.p: Other normocytic causes: heart failure, thyroid, cortisol or androgen deficiency, pregnancy, cancer, marrow infiltration (myelophthisic), old age, HIV.

table: B12 deficiency, folate deficiency, inherited metabolic disease
Reticulocytosis, marrow aplasia, liver disease, drugs and toxins

items.p: In megaloblastic anemia DNA synthesis is impaired, so the nucleus matures more slowly than the cytoplasm: large cells with large, immature nuclei.
Smear: hypersegmented neutrophils, large red cells of varying size, sometimes pancytopenia.
Drugs that cause macrocytosis through DNA metabolism include zidovudine, hydroxyurea, methotrexate, azathioprine and capecitabine.

items.note: Slide 27 lists hypothyroidism under "lipid abnormalities" while slide 44 calls its mechanism unclear.

items.p: B12 needs intrinsic factor from the stomach and a receptor in the ileum.

table: Strict vegetarians, breastfed infants of vegan mothers
Ileal resection, Crohn's disease, Imerslund–Gräsbeck syndrome

items.p: Metformin lowers B12.

Anemia, glossitis, poor appetite and gut symptoms occur in both deficiencies. Numbness and reduced cognition occur only with B12. Cobalamin under 200 pg/mL; homocysteine and methylmalonic acid both high.

ul: Severe or symptomatic anemia, neurologic symptoms, malabsorption or poor adherence: intramuscular 1000 mcg, 1–3 times weekly or daily in week 1, then weekly for up to 4 weeks
Otherwise: weekly injections for 4 weeks then monthly cyanocobalamin (or hydroxocobalamin every 3 months), or 1000–2000 mcg by mouth daily
Marrow recovers within hours; reticulocytes peak at 1 week; counts and MCV normal in 2–3 months; nerves take up to a year

items.note: Slide 33 lists "nitric oxide" as a cause; the standard cause is nitrous oxide. The amounts "1 mg" and "100 mg" beside "Nutritional" are not explained on the slide.

items.p: Develops faster than B12 deficiency.

ul: Poor diet, alcohol
Higher demand: hemolytic anemia, pregnancy, hemodialysis, dermatitis
Malabsorption: celiac disease, tropical sprue, jejunal resection, severe Crohn's disease, short gut, sulfasalazine
Methotrexate

items.p: The blood picture is the same as in B12 deficiency, with no nerve damage. Deficiency in pregnancy raises the risk of neural tube defects.
Serum folate under 2 ng/mL fits deficiency; over 4 makes it unlikely. Homocysteine is high; methylmalonic acid is normal.

ul: Myelodysplastic syndrome: ineffective erythropoiesis in a hypercellular marrow. Anemia is the most common cytopenia; enlarged organs and nodes are uncommon. Smear: dysplastic nucleated red cells, basophilic stippling, bilobed pseudo-Pelger–Huët neutrophils.

Alcohol and liver disease: anemia in 75% of chronic liver disease. Alcohol suppresses red cell production and EPO and reduces B12 absorption; varices bleed; a congested spleen and altered membrane lipids (spur cells) shorten survival.
Hypothyroidism: mechanism unclear; may resolve with thyroxine.

cards.q: Lecture definition of anemia
cards.a: Low red cell mass or hemoglobin: Hb more than 2 SD below the mean for age and sex (judged against oxygen demand)

cards.q: Three critical aspects in working up anemia
cards.a: Clinical history, CBC with reticulocyte count, peripheral smear

cards.q: Anemia with a raised reticulocyte count means...
cards.a: Hemolysis or blood loss

cards.q: MCV groups and the first test in each
cards.a: < 80 microcytic: ferritin. 80–100 normocytic: reticulocytes. > 100 macrocytic: megaloblastic or not.

cards.q: Normocytic anemia with low reticulocytes: causes
cards.a: Anemia of chronic disease, kidney disease, early iron deficiency, primary marrow disorders (leukemia, MDS, MPN), drugs

cards.q: Mechanism of anemia of chronic disease
cards.a: IL-6 raises hepcidin, which blocks ferroportin in duodenum and macrophages; plasma iron falls within hours

cards.q: Iron deficiency versus anemia of chronic disease: the discriminating tests
cards.a: Iron deficiency: high TIBC, low ferritin, high RDW, hepcidin suppressed. Chronic disease: normal or low TIBC, normal or high ferritin, normal RDW, hepcidin high.

cards.q: Goal of treatment in anemia of chronic disease
cards.a: Treat the underlying condition to relieve symptoms, not to normalize hemoglobin; iron only if truly deficient

cards.q: When to transfuse in anemia of chronic disease (lecturer's note)
cards.a: Hemoglobin under 7 g/dL, or a symptomatic patient at any hemoglobin

cards.q: Anemia of chronic kidney disease: mechanisms
cards.a: Low EPO, reduced renal clearance of hepcidin, uremic inhibitors, shortened red cell survival

cards.q: Anemia of CKD on dialysis: order of treatment and target
cards.a: Correct iron deficiency first, then ESA first line; target hemoglobin 10–11.5 g/dL

cards.q: Pure red cell aplasia: definition
cards.a: Severe anemia with very low reticulocytes (often < 10,000/µL) and virtual absence of erythroid precursors in the marrow

cards.q: Congenital pure red cell aplasia
cards.a: Diamond–Blackfan anemia (usually high MCV)

cards.q: Marrow clue to parvovirus B19 and how to confirm
cards.a: Giant proerythroblasts (suggestive, not diagnostic); confirm with parvovirus B19 PCR

cards.q: Megaloblastic versus non-megaloblastic macrocytosis: MCV
cards.a: Megaloblastic usually > 110 fL; non-megaloblastic usually < 105 fL

cards.q: What makes a cell megaloblastic?
cards.a: Impaired DNA synthesis: the nucleus matures more slowly than the cytoplasm (nuclear-cytoplasmic dyssynchrony)

cards.q: Smear in megaloblastic anemia
cards.a: Hypersegmented neutrophils, macrocytes of varying size, sometimes pancytopenia

cards.q: B12 deficiency: causes by mechanism
cards.a: Diet (vegans), no intrinsic factor (gastrectomy, pernicious anemia), competition (fish tapeworm, blind loop), no receptor (ileal resection, Crohn's, Imerslund–Gräsbeck)

cards.q: What separates B12 deficiency from folate deficiency clinically?
cards.a: Neuropsychological symptoms (numbness, reduced cognition) occur only in B12 deficiency

cards.q: Homocysteine and methylmalonic acid in B12 versus folate deficiency
cards.a: B12: both high. Folate: homocysteine high, methylmalonic acid normal.

cards.q: When is B12 given by intensive intramuscular course?
cards.a: Symptomatic or severe anemia, neuropsychiatric symptoms, possible malabsorption, concern about adherence

cards.q: Response to B12 treatment: timeline
cards.a: Marrow within hours; reticulocyte peak at 1 week; counts and MCV normal in 2–3 months; nerves up to a year

cards.q: Folate deficiency: main causes
cards.a: Poor diet and alcohol; increased demand (hemolysis, pregnancy, hemodialysis); malabsorption (celiac, tropical sprue, jejunal resection); methotrexate, sulfasalazine

cards.q: Serum folate cutoffs
cards.a: > 4 ng/mL: deficiency unlikely. < 2 ng/mL: consistent with deficiency.

cards.q: Folate deficiency in pregnancy raises the risk of...
cards.a: Fetal neural tube defects

cards.q: Myelodysplastic syndrome: key features
cards.a: Ineffective erythropoiesis with a hypercellular marrow; anemia is the most common cytopenia; pseudo-Pelger–Huët neutrophils, basophilic stippling

cards.q: Why is anemia common in alcoholic liver disease?
cards.a: Suppressed red cell and EPO production, reduced B12 absorption, variceal bleeding, congestive splenomegaly and altered membrane lipids (spur cells)

questions.stem: Which is NOT among the listed clinical manifestations of anemia?
questions.explanation: Listed: tiredness, weakness, shortness of breath, pale or yellowish skin, palpitations, dizziness, chest pain, cold hands and feet, headaches. A: Listed. C: Listed. D: Listed. E: Listed.

questions.stem: How are the two classic approaches to anemia (mechanism and red cell size) meant to be used?

options.A: Size first, with mechanism decided after a marrow biopsy
options.B: Mechanism first, with size reserved for microcytic cases
options.C: Both considered together, with the MCV and reticulocyte count
options.D: Size in adults and mechanism in children under 12 years
options.E: Ferritin first, with size and mechanism in unclear cases

questions.explanation: In reality production/loss/breakdown and MCV are considered simultaneously; the lecturer's note says to look at the MCV and the reticulocyte count. A: Both are considered at once. B: Both are considered at once. D: No such split is made. E: Ferritin comes after the MCV in microcytosis.

questions.stem: Which pairing of index and meaning is correct?

options.B: MCHC: average hemoglobin content of each red cell
options.C: RDW: variation in hemoglobin content of red cells
options.D: MCHC: average hemoglobin concentration per red cell
options.E: MCV: variation in the volume of the red cells

questions.explanation: MCV is the average volume, MCH the average hemoglobin content, MCHC the average hemoglobin concentration, and RDW the variation in red cell size. A: MCH is the average hemoglobin content. B: That is the MCH. C: RDW measures variation in size. E: MCV is the average volume.

questions.stem: According to the lecturer's handwritten note, a raised RDW in an anemic patient makes which diagnosis more likely?
questions.explanation: The note reads: high RDW = high chance of iron deficiency. The table on slide 17 also gives a raised RDW in iron deficiency and a normal RDW in anemia of chronic disease. A: Not what the note says. B: The RDW is normal in the comparison table. C: Not what the note says. D: Not what the note says.

questions.explanation: The algorithm starts with the reticulocyte count: normal or decreased → MCV; increased → hemolysis or blood loss. B: The second step when reticulocytes are not raised. C: For microcytic anemia. D: Essential, but not the first branch. E: Not a first step.

options.A: Clinical history, CBC with reticulocytes, marrow biopsy
options.B: Clinical history, CBC with reticulocytes, peripheral smear

questions.stem: In that algorithm, anemia with an increased reticulocyte count points to:
questions.explanation: An increased reticulocyte count means hemolysis (extrinsic or intrinsic to the red cell) or blood loss. A: Marrow invasion has a normal or low count. B: Renal disease has a normal or low count. C: B12 deficiency has a normal or low count. E: Thalassemia sits in the microcytic group.

questions.stem: Which condition is listed under normocytic anemia with a normal or decreased reticulocyte count?
questions.explanation: Normocytic: TEC (transient erythroblastopenia of childhood), early ACD, renal and thyroid disease, marrow invasion. A: Listed under microcytic. B: Listed under macrocytic. D: Listed under macrocytic. E: Listed under microcytic.

questions.stem: Where does anemia of chronic disease appear in the MCV groups of the algorithm?
questions.explanation: ACD (early) is in the normocytic group and ACD (late) in the microcytic group. B: Reversed. C: It does not become macrocytic. D: Not as shown. E: It is listed as microcytic when late.

questions.stem: Which order of erythroid maturation is correct?

options.A: Proerythroblast, nuclear extrusion, erythroblast stages, reticulocyte
options.B: Erythroblast stages, proerythroblast, nuclear extrusion, reticulocyte
options.C: Proerythroblast, erythroblast stages, reticulocyte, nuclear extrusion
options.D: Reticulocyte, proerythroblast, erythroblast stages, nuclear extrusion
options.E: Proerythroblast, erythroblast stages, nuclear extrusion, reticulocyte

B: The proerythroblast comes first. C: The reticulocyte has no nucleus. D: The reticulocyte is the last step before the red cell.

questions.stem: The lecturer's note on the step from reticulocyte to red cell names what the reticulocyte still carries. What is it?
questions.explanation: The handwritten note marks ribosomes at the reticulocyte-to-red-cell step. B: Extruded before the reticulocyte stage. C: Denatured hemoglobin, not a normal content. D: Not what the note says. E: Not what the note says.

questions.stem: Which timing of red cell production and survival is shown?

options.A: About 1 week in the marrow; 120 days in blood
options.B: About 3 weeks in the marrow; 90 days in blood
options.C: About 3 days in the marrow; 120 days in blood
options.D: About 3 weeks in the marrow; 120 days in blood
options.E: About 3 months in the marrow; 3 weeks in blood

questions.stem: As the hematocrit falls from 45% to 15%, what happens to red cell precursors?

options.A: Marrow time lengthens and blood reticulocyte time shortens
options.B: Marrow time shortens and blood reticulocyte time lengthens
options.C: Marrow time and blood reticulocyte time both shorten
options.D: Marrow time and blood reticulocyte time both lengthen
options.E: Marrow time is unchanged and blood reticulocyte time lengthens

questions.explanation: With worsening anemia, normoblasts and reticulocytes spend less time in the marrow (3.5 to 1.5 days) and reticulocytes more time in blood (1.0 to 2.5 days). A: Reversed. C: Blood time lengthens. D: Marrow time shortens. E: Marrow time falls from 3.5 to 1.5 days.

questions.stem: At a hematocrit of 15%, how long do reticulocytes spend in the blood?
questions.explanation: Blood reticulocyte time rises from 1.0 day (hematocrit 45%) to 2.5 days (hematocrit 15%). A: The value at a hematocrit of 45%. B: The value at a hematocrit of 35% (and the marrow time at 15%). D: The value at a hematocrit of 25%. E: The marrow time at a hematocrit of 45%.

questions.stem: An anemic patient has a low reticulocyte count and an MCV of 72 fL. Which test comes next?
questions.explanation: Microcytic anemia (MCV < 80 fL): check ferritin; low ferritin = iron deficiency. A: For macrocytic anemia. B: Not the first test. C: For hemolysis. D: Not the first test.

questions.stem: Which is NOT among the causes of microcytic anemia with a normal or high ferritin?
questions.explanation: Normal or high ferritin: chronic disease, thalassemias, hemoglobinopathies, lead intoxication, sideroblastic anemia. A: Listed. B: Listed. C: Listed. E: Listed.

questions.stem: A patient has a normocytic anemia with an absolute reticulocyte count of 180,000/µL. Which cause fits?
questions.explanation: Normocytic anemia with reticulocytes > 100,000/µL: bleeding or hemolysis. A: Low reticulocytes. B: Very low reticulocytes. C: Low reticulocytes. D: Low reticulocytes.

questions.stem: Which is given as an example of a primary bone marrow disorder causing normocytic anemia with low reticulocytes?
questions.explanation: Primary bone marrow disorders: leukemias, MDS, MPN; drugs are listed in the same box. A: An example of anemia of chronic disease. B: Listed with anemia of chronic disease. D: High reticulocytes. E: High reticulocytes.

questions.stem: Beyond the traditional infectious, inflammatory and neoplastic causes, the lecture links anemia of chronic disease to:

options.B: Obesity, diabetes, heart failure, critical illness, severe trauma

options.B: Hemoglobin 7 to 11 g/dL, normal MCV, high reticulocytes

questions.stem: In inflammation, IL-6 makes the liver release hepcidin. Which protein does hepcidin block?
questions.explanation: IL-6 raises liver hepcidin, which blocks ferroportin in the duodenum, iron-recycling macrophages and hepatocytes, so plasma iron falls. A: Not the target. B: Not the target named. C: Storage protein. E: Not the target.

questions.stem: How soon does hypoferremia develop in inflammation?
questions.explanation: Hypoferremia develops within the first few hours. B: It is faster. C: It is faster. D: It is faster. E: Stores are not empty in inflammation.

questions.stem: Besides interleukin-6, what raises hepcidin in the figures on inflammation and kidney disease?

options.A: Impaired liver function reducing hepcidin breakdown
options.D: Duodenal iron loading increasing hepcidin uptake
options.E: Impaired renal function reducing hepcidin clearance

questions.stem: A woman with active rheumatoid arthritis has Hb 10 g/dL and MCV 78 fL. Which iron study result would point to coexisting iron deficiency rather than anemia of chronic inflammation alone?
questions.explanation: Transferrin (TIBC) is increased in iron deficiency and normal or decreased in anemia of chronic inflammation; MCV, iron and saturation can be low in both. A: Low in both. B: Low in both. D: Fits inflammation. E: Fits inflammation.

questions.stem: Which finding fits anemia of chronic inflammation rather than iron deficiency?
questions.explanation: Anemia of chronic inflammation: hepcidin increased, ferritin normal or increased, RDW normal. Iron deficiency: hepcidin suppressed, ferritin low, RDW increased. A: Iron deficiency. C: Iron deficiency. D: Iron deficiency. E: Iron deficiency.

questions.stem: What is the stated goal of managing anemia of chronic disease?

options.A: Treat the underlying condition and add oral iron until the hemoglobin is normal

questions.explanation: Do not give iron unless the patient is iron deficient; ESAs can be given; transfuse for Hb < 7 g/dL or a symptomatic patient. A: Not without iron deficiency. B: Not without iron deficiency. C: Not without iron deficiency. E: Not without iron deficiency.

questions.explanation: On dialysis, treat absolute or functional iron deficiency first; once iron replete, ESAs are first line. A: Replace iron first. C: Not the first step. D: Not indicated. E: Not the first step.

questions.explanation: Pure red cell aplasia: severe anemia, reticulocytes often < 10,000/µL, virtual absence of erythroid precursors in the marrow. B: Megaloblastic anemia. C: Sideroblastic anemia. D: Not this picture. E: Expected with high reticulocytes.

options.C: EPO antibodies after treatment with ESAs

options.C: It is directly cytotoxic to red cell precursors
options.D: It triggers immune attack after thymoma

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with HIV has hemoglobin 6.1 g/dL, reticulocytes 4,000/µL, and normal white cells and platelets. The marrow shows almost no erythroid precursors and a few giant proerythroblasts. What is the best next step?

options.B: CT of the chest for thymoma

questions.explanation: Giant proerythroblasts are strongly suggestive of parvovirus infection but not diagnostic, so PCR for parvovirus B19 is done. B: The marrow finding points to parvovirus first. C: The marrow is not megaloblastic. D: Reticulocytes are absent; this is not hemolysis. E: Would not identify the cause.

questions.stem: Which endocrine deficiencies are listed as causes of normocytic anemia?
questions.explanation: Endocrine disorders: thyroid hormone, cortisol and androgen deficiencies. A: Insulin and estrogens are not listed. C: Not the three listed. D: Parathyroid hormone is not listed. E: Aldosterone is not listed.

questions.stem: Which is NOT listed among the other causes of normocytic anemia?
questions.explanation: Other causes: heart failure, endocrine disorders, pregnancy, cancer, myelophthisic anemia, anemia in older patients, HIV infection. Folate deficiency is macrocytic. A: Listed. B: Listed. D: Listed. E: Listed.

questions.stem: Above which MCV does a macrocytic anemia usually point to a megaloblastic cause?
questions.explanation: Macrocytic (MCV > 100) is not the same as megaloblastic: megaloblastic causes usually give MCV > 110 fL; others usually < 105 fL. A: The cut-off for macrocytosis. B: Normal range. C: Non-megaloblastic causes usually stay below this. D: Too high.

questions.stem: Which cause of macrocytosis is grouped with folate and B12 deficiency under defective DNA synthesis?
questions.explanation: Megaloblastic: folate deficiency, vitamin B12 deficiency, inherited metabolic disease. Non-megaloblastic: hemolysis/reticulocytosis, marrow hypo/aplasia, liver disease, drugs/toxins. B: Non-megaloblastic. C: Non-megaloblastic. D: Non-megaloblastic. E: Listed on the non-megaloblastic side.

questions.stem: Each of these drugs is listed as causing macrocytosis through abnormal DNA metabolism EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Listed: antiretrovirals (zidovudine), azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine, capecitabine, cladribine, cytosine arabinoside, hydroxyurea, imatinib, sunitinib, methotrexate. A: Listed. B: Listed. C: Listed. E: Listed.

questions.stem: Which causes macrocytosis by a shift to immature or stressed red cells?
questions.explanation: Shift to immature or stressed red cells: reticulocytosis and the action of erythropoietin (skip macrocytes, stress erythrocytosis). A: Abnormal DNA metabolism. C: Abnormal DNA metabolism. D: A primary marrow disorder. E: A lipid abnormality.

questions.stem: In the table of mechanisms of macrocytosis, liver disease is placed under:
questions.explanation: Lipid abnormalities: liver disease (the table also puts hypothyroidism here). A: B12, folate and drugs. B: Reticulocytosis and erythropoietin. C: Aplastic anemia, MDS and others. E: Alcohol abuse and myeloma.

questions.stem: Which pair is listed under "mechanism unknown" in the table of macrocytosis?

options.B: Aplastic anemia and red cell aplasia

questions.explanation: Mechanism unknown: alcohol abuse, multiple myeloma and other plasma cell disorders. A: Liver disease is under lipid abnormalities. B: Primary marrow disorders. C: Shift to immature red cells. D: LGL leukemia is a primary marrow disorder.

questions.stem: What is the basic defect in megaloblastic anemia?
questions.explanation: A nutrient needed for DNA synthesis is lacking, so the nucleus lags behind the cytoplasm (nuclear-cytoplasmic dyssynchrony). B: Microcytic anemias. C: Not the defect. D: Not the basic defect. E: Anemia of inflammation.

questions.stem: A patient with a low vitamin B12 has an MCV of 120 fL. Which white cell change is expected on the smear?
questions.explanation: Megaloblastic smear: hypersegmented neutrophils, macrocytosis with variable red cells, occasionally pancytopenia. A: Infection. B: Infection. D: Acute myeloid leukemia. E: CLL.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old vegan has an MCV of 112 fL and numb feet. Which test result is expected?
questions.explanation: B12 is needed for methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA and homocysteine → methionine, so both MMA and homocysteine rise. In folate deficiency MMA is normal. A: Raised in B12 deficiency. C: Ineffective erythropoiesis raises LDH. D: Low before treatment. E: Not expected.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man had a total gastrectomy 6 years ago. He has numbness of both feet, poor concentration and an MCV of 118 fL. Which mechanism explains his deficiency?

options.A: Loss of the ileal receptor for the complex
options.B: Loss of jejunal surface for folate uptake
options.C: Competition for the vitamin by gut bacteria
options.D: Loss of intrinsic factor needed for ileal uptake
options.E: Lack of the plasma carrier transcobalamin II

questions.explanation: Gastrectomy and autoimmune gastritis cause intrinsic factor deficiency. Numbness and reduced cognition point to B12 rather than folate. A: The ileum is intact. B: Folate deficiency has no neurologic signs. C: That is the blind loop mechanism. E: A rare inherited cause.

questions.stem: Which groups have nutritional vitamin B12 deficiency?

options.A: Strict vegetarians and patients with hemolytic anemia
options.B: Malnourished adults and patients on hemodialysis
options.C: Pregnant women and patients with dermatitis
options.E: Strict vegetarians and breastfed infants of vegan mothers

questions.explanation: Nutritional B12 deficiency: strict vegetarians and breastfed infants of vegan mothers. A: Hemolysis raises folate demand. B: Listed for folate. C: Listed for folate. D: Not listed for B12.

questions.stem: How does pernicious anemia cause B12 deficiency?

options.A: Autoimmune gastritis with ileal receptor deficiency
options.B: Autoimmune gastritis with intrinsic factor loss
options.C: Autoimmune ileitis with intrinsic factor deficiency
options.D: Chronic gastritis with competition for B12

questions.explanation: "IF deficiency": gastrectomy and autoimmune gastritis (pernicious anemia). A: The receptor defect is a separate group. C: The disease is gastric. D: Competition is fish tapeworm or blind loop. E: Listed separately under other causes.

questions.stem: Which pair causes B12 deficiency by competition?

options.A: Fish tapeworm and intestinal blind loop

questions.explanation: Competition: fish tapeworm and intestinal blind loop. B: Ileal resection is a receptor deficiency. C: Gastrectomy is intrinsic factor deficiency. D: Tropical sprue is listed for folate. E: Autoimmune gastritis is intrinsic factor deficiency.

questions.stem: Which causes are grouped as "receptor deficiency"?

options.B: Ileal resection, autoimmune gastritis, transcobalamin II deficiency
options.C: Ileal resection, Crohn's disease, Imerslund–Gräsbeck syndrome
options.D: Jejunal resection, Crohn's disease, tropical sprue
options.E: Ileal resection, fish tapeworm, intestinal blind loop

questions.explanation: Receptor deficiency: ileal resection, Crohn's disease, Imerslund–Gräsbeck syndrome (autosomal recessive). A: Gastrectomy is intrinsic factor deficiency. B: Different groups. D: The folate malabsorption list. E: The last two are competition.

questions.stem: The lecturer's note on the treatment slide says Glucophage (metformin) lowers which level?
questions.explanation: The handwritten note: Glucophage lowers B12. B: Not what the note says. C: Not what the note says. D: Not what the note says. E: Not what the note says.

questions.stem: Which feature is specific to cobalamin deficiency and not seen with folate deficiency?
questions.explanation: Neuropsychological symptoms are specific to cobalamin deficiency. The lecturer's note: B12 gives numbness and reduced cognition. A: Not marked as specific. B: Not marked as specific. C: Not marked as specific. E: The blood picture is the same in both.

questions.stem: Which cobalamin level is given for the diagnosis of deficiency?
questions.explanation: Cobalamin level < 200 pg/mL. A: The figure is 200. B: The figure is 200. D: The figure is 200. E: The figure is 200.

questions.stem: Each of the following is a "concerning feature" that calls for initial intramuscular B12 EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Concerning features: symptomatic or severe anemia, neuropsychiatric symptoms, possible malabsorption, concern about adherence. A: Listed. B: Listed. C: Listed. D: Listed.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with pernicious anemia has paresthesias and a cobalamin of 120 pg/mL. How is B12 given at first?
questions.explanation: With concerning features: 1000 mcg IM 1 to 3 times weekly or daily in week 1, then weekly up to 4 weeks; repeat CBC at 2 to 3 weeks. A: Concerning features need IM. C: Does not treat B12 deficiency. D: Not the regimen. E: Too infrequent at first.

questions.stem: For how long may the initial intramuscular course be continued if neurologic symptoms are improving?
questions.explanation: Duration is typically 4 weeks; if neuropsychiatric or neurologic symptoms are improving it may be continued for up to 3 months. B: The typical duration without that extension. C: Not the figure given. D: Not the figure given. E: Not the figure given.

questions.stem: After 4 weekly intramuscular doses in a patient without concerning features, which maintenance is given?
questions.explanation: IM 1000 mcg weekly for 4 weeks, followed by cyanocobalamin once every month or hydroxocobalamin once every 3 months. A: Reversed. B: Not the intervals given. C: Hydroxocobalamin is given once in 3 months. E: Not the intervals given.

questions.stem: What is the oral or sublingual dose of B12 for patients without concerning features?
questions.explanation: Oral or sublingual: 1000 to 2000 mcg daily, monitoring the CBC and B12 level at 4 to 8 weeks, at 6 months, then annually. A: The dose is daily. B: Ten times too low. C: That is the dietary intake in the absorption figure. D: Far too low.

questions.stem: A patient starts vitamin B12 for megaloblastic anemia. When do reticulocytes peak?
questions.explanation: After B12, megaloblastic changes resolve within hours; reticulocytes peak after 1 week; counts and MCV normalize in 2 to 3 months. A: Marrow changes resolve within hours. B: Earlier. D: When counts normalize. E: Later.

questions.stem: According to the lecturer's note, how fast do problems improve after treating B12 deficiency?

options.A: Reticulocytes within a few hours; neural problems within a week
options.B: Reticulocytes within a few weeks; neural problems within a year
options.C: Reticulocytes within a year; neural problems within a few weeks
options.D: Reticulocytes within a few weeks; neural problems within a month
options.E: Reticulocytes and neural problems both within a few weeks

questions.explanation: The note: in B12 deficiency reticulocytes improve within a few weeks, neural issues within a year. A: Neural recovery is slow. C: Reversed. D: Neural recovery takes up to a year. E: Neural recovery takes up to a year.

questions.stem: Which malabsorptive cause is listed under folate deficiency?
questions.explanation: Folate malabsorption: gluten-sensitive enteropathy, tropical sprue, jejunal resection, severe Crohn's disease, short gut syndrome, sulfasalazine. A: Listed for B12. B: Listed for B12. C: Listed for B12. E: Listed for B12.

questions.stem: How are two drugs classified among the causes of folate deficiency?
questions.explanation: Sulfasalazine is listed under malabsorption; methotrexate under other causes as an anti-folate drug, with alcohol. A: Reversed. B: Metformin was noted for B12. C: Hydroxyurea is not on this slide. D: Sulfasalazine is under malabsorption.

questions.stem: Which set lists states of increased folate demand or requirement?

options.A: Hemolytic anemia, pregnancy, gastrectomy, vegan diet
options.D: Hemolytic anemia, lactation, peritoneal dialysis, obesity

questions.explanation: Increased demand: hemolytic anemias; increased requirements: pregnancy, hemodialysis, dermatitis. A: The last two are B12 causes. C: Iron deficiency and hypothyroidism are not listed. D: Not as listed. E: Aplastic anemia has low red cell turnover.

questions.stem: Compared with B12 deficiency, the lecturer noted that folate deficiency:

options.A: Develops slower; look for it in pregnancy and dialysis
options.B: Develops faster; look for it in strict vegetarians
options.C: Develops faster; look for it in pregnancy and dialysis
options.D: Develops slower; look for it after ileal resection
options.E: Develops at the same rate; look for it in the elderly

questions.explanation: The note: folate deficiency occurs faster than B12 deficiency; look for it in pregnant and hemodialysis patients. A: It occurs faster. B: Vegetarians are at risk of B12 deficiency. D: Ileal resection is a B12 cause. E: It occurs faster.

questions.stem: Which feature separates cobalamin deficiency from folate deficiency?
questions.explanation: The blood picture is the same, but folate deficiency does not cause neuropsychiatric problems such as subacute combined degeneration. B: Both. C: Both. D: Both. E: Both.

questions.stem: Folate deficiency is strongly implicated in a higher incidence of:
questions.explanation: Folate deficiency is strongly implicated in increasing the incidence of fetal neural tube defects. A: Not the association stated. B: Neuropathy belongs to B12 deficiency. C: Not the association stated. D: Not the association stated.

questions.stem: How is the serum folate interpreted?

options.A: > 2 ng/mL: deficiency unlikely; < 1 ng/mL: consistent with deficiency
options.B: > 4 ng/mL: deficiency unlikely; < 3 ng/mL: consistent with deficiency
options.C: > 10 ng/mL: deficiency unlikely; < 4 ng/mL: consistent with deficiency
options.D: > 4 ng/mL: deficiency unlikely; < 2 ng/mL: consistent with deficiency
options.E: > 20 ng/mL: deficiency unlikely; < 10 ng/mL: consistent with deficiency

questions.explanation: Serum folate > 4 ng/mL makes deficiency unlikely; < 2 ng/mL is consistent with folate deficiency. A: The cutoffs are 4 and 2. B: The lower cutoff is 2. C: The cutoffs are 4 and 2. E: The cutoffs are 4 and 2.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man who drinks heavily and eats poorly has fatigue. Hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL, MCV 114 fL, hypersegmented neutrophils; neurologic examination is normal. Homocysteine is high and methylmalonic acid is normal. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: In folate deficiency homocysteine is high and MMA is normal; alcohol and malnutrition are listed causes, and there are no neurologic signs. A: Methylmalonic acid would be high. C: Does not give this metabolite pattern. D: Not megaloblastic; MCV usually < 105 fL. E: Not megaloblastic.

questions.stem: Which cytopenia is the most common in myelodysplastic syndrome?
questions.explanation: In MDS, anemia is the most common cytopenia; organomegaly and systemic symptoms are uncommon. A: Less common. B: Less common. D: Less common. E: Less common.

questions.stem: Which neutrophil finding on the lecture's smears belongs to myelodysplastic syndrome?
questions.explanation: The MDS smear shows a bilobed pseudo-Pelger–Huët (Pelgeroid) neutrophil nucleus; dysplastic nucleated red cells and basophilic stippling are also shown. B: Megaloblastic anemia. C: Not shown. D: The giant cell shown is a proerythroblast in parvovirus infection. E: Stippling was shown in red cells.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old has a macrocytic anemia with low reticulocytes. The marrow is hypercellular, with dysplastic red cell precursors. What explains the anemia?
questions.explanation: MDS: ineffective erythropoiesis, a hypercellular marrow with few red cells reaching the blood. A: The marrow is hypercellular. B: Reticulocytes would be high. C: Not suggested. D: Dysplasia points to MDS.

questions.stem: Anemia is found in what share of patients with chronic liver disease?
questions.explanation: Anemia is found in 75% of patients with chronic liver disease; it is multifactorial (underproduction, blood loss from esophageal varices, increased destruction). A: Too low. B: Too low. D: Too low. E: Too high.

questions.stem: Ethanol and its metabolites are said to do each of the following EXCEPT:

options.B: Increase hepcidin release from the liver

questions.explanation: Ethanol and its metabolites directly inhibit erythroid production and EPO production and decrease vitamin B12 absorption. A: Stated. C: Stated. D: Stated. E: Stated.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis and a large spleen has Hb 9.1 g/dL, MCV 103 fL, raised reticulocytes and red cells with irregular spiky projections. What are these cells?
questions.explanation: Liver disease: congestive splenomegaly, abnormal red cell metabolism and altered membrane lipids shorten survival; spur cell anemia. A: Regular projections. B: Fragments. C: G6PD deficiency. E: Marrow fibrosis.

questions.stem: What does the lecture say about macrocytosis in hypothyroidism?

options.A: Mechanism unclear and multifactorial; may resolve with thyroxine
options.B: Mechanism is B12 malabsorption; resolves with intramuscular B12
options.C: Mechanism is reticulocytosis; resolves when hemolysis stops
options.D: Mechanism is marrow fibrosis; persists despite thyroxine
options.E: Mechanism is folate loss; resolves with folic acid tablets

questions.explanation: Macrocytosis in hypothyroidism: mechanism unclear, multifactorial; it might resolve with thyroxine. B: Not what the slide says. C: Not what the slide says. D: It might resolve with thyroxine. E: Not what the slide says.
